Volume 11 · Chapter 04

Market risk and portfolio loss

Advanced Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v11-c03

By the endCompare risk measures and state their information and distributional limitations.

Measure a loss distribution without mistaking it for protection

Capability. Define a portfolio's loss, calculate value at risk and expected shortfall with probability atoms, derive their central properties, and test dependence, horizon and backtesting assumptions. The local prerequisite is credit underwriting: a repayment forecast, a contractual payment and cash available at a deadline are different objects. We also use expectation and covariance, sampling distributions, portfolio risk and nonlinear revaluation and hedging.

Merrow Risk Office receives two summaries. Each loan sleeve has a 95% value at risk of zero, yet the combined portfolio has a 95% value at risk of 100 CU. A second portfolio has the same value at risk before and after its worst loss increases tenfold. Neither calculation is necessarily wrong. A quantile answers a narrower question than a worst loss, a tail average or a funding requirement. This chapter derives those distinctions and supplies an original finite-scenario laboratory. Every probability, loss and policy example is synthetic; none is current market data, a capital regulation or an investment recommendation.

1. Specify the loss before calculating its distribution

Fix the portfolio, currency, information available at date t, liquidation or valuation horizon h, cash-flow treatment and trading policy. A convenient funded loss, in currency units at t + h, is

Lh = VtB(t,t+h) − Vt+h − ΣjCjB(tj,t+h).

V is the portfolio's marked value; positive C is a receipt from the portfolio, negative C a payment; B(a,b) is the stipulated accumulation factor. The sum includes the relevant cash flows between t and t + h. Initial funding and later cash must use the same convention. For a dynamic strategy, include every external contribution and withdrawal, transaction cost and financing cost consistently; do not count trades once as changes in V and again as unfinanced cash. An alternative unfinanced mark loss is legitimate if labeled. Positive L means a loss; a negative loss is a gain. Present-value and terminal-value losses differ by discounting, even for the same portfolio.

Risk normally concerns a conditional physical law P(Lh ≤ x | information at t), not the pricing law Q used inside a valuation model. One can revalue each simulated future state using a pricing model and still assign those future states physical probabilities. Treating Q probabilities as forecast frequencies is an additional assumption. Historical samples, fitted factor laws and judgmental scenarios are different sources of evidence; their labels should survive aggregation.

A full revaluation maps each joint scenario into all contractual cash and terminal marks. A local delta or delta-gamma approximation is a separate approximation whose errors can be large near exercise thresholds, defaults or large price changes. Positions must share compatible horizon and currency conventions before their losses are added. Do not add currency percentages to CU losses, double count a credit write-down already inside a price mark, or assume a frozen-position experiment describes an actively managed portfolio.

Worked example 1 — A funded bond horizon

A default-free zero pays 100 CU in two years. Today its price is 100/1.05². Fund its purchase for one year at a known gross factor of 1.05, then sell it with one year remaining. There are no interim cash flows. If the one-year yield at sale is y, the date-1 funded loss is 100/1.05 − 100/(1+y). At y = 5%, the loss is zero: the bond's increase in value exactly pays funding. At y = 10%, loss is 100/1.05 − 100/1.10 = 1000/231 ≈ 4.329004 CU. At y = 0, loss is −100/21 ≈ −4.761905 CU.

For a yield change d from 5%, the local loss approximation at the sale horizon is 100d/1.05². At d = 0.05 it predicts 2000/441 ≈ 4.535147 CU. Subtracting this from the full loss gives exactly −100d²/[1.05²(1.05+d)], provided 1.05+d > 0. This signed remainder shows the approximation overstates the loss in this particular convex bond case; it is not a universal direction for nonlinear portfolios. Using the original two-year duration without accounting for the one-year horizon would introduce another error.

If a collateral payment of 6 CU is due tomorrow and no cash or borrowing is available then, a favorable sale price next year does not fund tomorrow's payment. A terminal loss distribution and a dated funding ladder answer different questions. Later chapters build the ladder explicitly.

2. Value at risk is a specified quantile

Let F(x) = P(L ≤ x) be the loss CDF under the chosen law. For 0 < α < 1, use the left-quantile convention

VaRα(L) = qα = inf{x : F(x) ≥ α}.

For a finite real-valued loss law, sort distinct losses and accumulate their probabilities; q is the first loss whose cumulative mass reaches α. A confidence of 0.99 is a probability level, not a 99% confidence interval for an estimated quantile. VaR has the units and horizon of L. It can be negative if sufficiently much probability lies in gains.

The quantile satisfies P(L > q) ≤ 1−α and P(L ≥ q) ≥ 1−α. Equality of the first probability need not hold when there is mass at q. A valid 99% VaR does not mean exactly one out of every hundred observations will exceed it, nor that an exceedance cannot be arbitrarily severe. If a portfolio loses 0 with probability 0.995 and M > 0 with probability 0.005, its 99% VaR is zero for every M. The tail severity can grow without changing that quantile.

For empirical quantiles in this chapter, each of n observations has mass 1/n and the same left-quantile rule applies: select ordered observation number ceil(nα). Interpolated sample-quantile conventions produce different answers and must be declared. Repeated losses remain probability atoms; dropping duplicates changes the empirical law unless their frequencies are retained. Estimated quantiles also have sampling and model uncertainty that the plug-in value does not display.

3. Expected shortfall fills a tail of exactly the requested probability

For an integrable loss, E|L| < ∞, define expected shortfall as the average of the upper quantiles:

ESα(L) = [1/(1−α)] ∫α1qu du
= qα + E[(L−qα)+]/(1−α).

In a finite distribution this is a probability-weighted mean of the worst 1−α mass. Include every loss strictly above q, then include exactly (1−α)−P(L > q) of the mass at q. This residual is nonnegative and no larger than the available mass at q. Multiplying the selected mass by its loss gives

ESα = {E[L 1{L>q}] + q[(1−α)−P(L>q)]}/(1−α).

Rearrange its numerator to obtain the positive-part formula. The quantile-integral definition agrees because the top quantiles spend precisely those lengths of probability at each finite loss. No literal sale or random destruction of part of a state is intended: fractional mass describes how to average the quantile tail. For a continuous distribution with F(q) = α and no atom at q, ES equals E[L | L > q]. With atoms, either strict or weak conditional-tail mean can be wrong.

These definitions and their general-distribution extension are supported by Rockafellar and Uryasev's author manuscript, 28 November 2001, published in 2002. We derive the finite formulas and proofs here. Their term conditional value at risk is used for the atom-adjusted tail measure; a label alone does not establish that another report uses the same definition.

Worked example 2 — The atom at the boundary matters

Merrow's original one-horizon desk loss
Loss CUProbabilityCumulative probability
00.900.90
100.050.95
1000.051.00

At α = 0.925, VaR is 10. The upper tail must have mass 0.075. It contains the full 0.05 at loss 100 and only 0.025 of the 0.05 at loss 10. Thus ES = (0.05×100 + 0.025×10)/0.075 = 70 CU. Equivalently, 10 + [0.05×90]/0.075 = 70. The strict conditional mean above VaR is 100; the weak conditional mean at or above VaR is (0.5+5)/0.10 = 55. Neither equals 70.

At α = 0.90, VaR is 0 and ES is 55. At α = 0.95, VaR is still 10, because F(10) reaches 0.95 exactly, but ES is 100. For any α strictly between 0.95 and 1, both VaR and ES are 100. A reported convention that silently moves the 0.95 quantile to 100 changes VaR while leaving this tail mean unchanged. Always check the boundary rule.

4. Two finite certificates explain what ES does

Let finite states i have probabilities pi > 0 summing to one and losses ℓi. Write τ = 1−α. Introduce a threshold θ, measured in CU, and the convex piecewise-linear function

f(θ) = θ + (1/τ)Σipi(ℓi−θ)+.

Each positive-part term is convex in θ, so f is convex. Below the smallest loss its slope is 1−1/τ < 0; above the greatest loss its slope is 1. A minimum is therefore attained in the finite loss range. Its left and right derivatives, including ties, are

f′−(θ) = 1−P(L ≥ θ)/τ,
f′+(θ) = 1−P(L > θ)/τ.

A convex piecewise-linear function is minimized exactly where the left slope is nonpositive and the right slope nonnegative. Hence a minimizing threshold satisfies P(L > θ) ≤ τ ≤ P(L ≥ θ). In particular the left quantile q minimizes f, and the atom formula proves minθ f(θ) = ESα. The minimizing threshold need not be unique: if α is exactly the cumulative mass at a loss and the next loss is larger, f is flat between them. ES is still a single number.

A second certificate expresses ES as a maximum over alternative weights on the same supplied states:

ESα(L) = max Σiwiℓi,
subject to Σiwi = 1 and 0 ≤ wi ≤ pi/τ.

For any feasible w and any θ, write Σwℓ = θ + Σw(ℓ−θ). Negative differences contribute at most zero; positive ones have weights at most p/τ. Thus Σwℓ ≤ f(θ), giving a bound without invoking an optimization theorem. To attain it at q, set w = p/τ above q, zero below q, and allocate the remaining total weight to the states at q. The quantile inequalities guarantee enough boundary capacity and a nonnegative remainder. This is exactly tail filling divided by τ. Both certificates agree, proving the maximum, minimum and tail average are equal.

In worked example 2 an attaining weight vector is (0, 1/3, 2/3). Its capacities are (12, 2/3, 2/3), its weights sum to one and its loss average is 70. Capacity 12 does not mean probability 12 is allowed: the weights must also be nonnegative and sum to one. The maximizing weights stress existing states within a density cap. They are not a newly estimated physical distribution and cannot reveal an omitted state.

The maximum representation proves four properties on a common finite probability space. If L ≤ M state by state, every feasible weighted average of L is at most that of M, so ES is monotone. Adding certain loss c adds c to every average; scaling losses by λ ≥ 0 scales ES by λ. For two jointly specified losses L and M, every feasible w satisfies Ew[L+M] ≤ maxvEv[L] + maxvEv[M]. Maximizing the left side proves subadditivity. These are the coherent-risk properties in the loss-sign convention. A risk-free receipt c reduces L and ES by c. Negative scaling reverses the loss ordering and is not covered by positive homogeneity.

These properties are mathematical discipline, not a guarantee that the chosen probabilities, position marks or missing-tail assumptions are correct. In particular, subadditivity compares risks under one joint law and the same α. It does not justify adding separately calculated tail losses at different dates, confidence levels or incompatible model vintages. Risk constraints, cash availability and accounting or regulatory capital remain distinct decisions.

5. Diversification needs a joint distribution

Worked example 3 — Same individual losses, different joint tails

Each of two sleeves loses 100 with physical probability 0.04 and otherwise loses zero. For either sleeve, 95% VaR is zero because F(0) = 0.96; ES is 0.04×100/0.05 = 80. Under independence, both lose with probability 0.0016, exactly one loses with total probability 0.0768, and neither loses with probability 0.9216. The portfolio therefore has VaR0.95 = 100, exceeding the sum of individual VaRs, which is zero. This is an exact counterexample to VaR subadditivity.

The portfolio's upper 0.05 mass contains 0.0016 at 200 and 0.0484 at 100. Its ES is (0.0016×200 + 0.0484×100)/0.05 = 103.2, below 80+80 = 160. Do not average only the double-loss state: that state occupies much less than the requested tail.

Now build a different joint law: with probability λ use a common Bernoulli event so both sleeves fail together; with probability 1−λ use the independent mechanism. Each marginal loss probability remains 0.04. At λ = 0.25, the joint probabilities are neither 0.9312, A only 0.0288, B only 0.0288 and both 0.0112. VaR stays 100, but ES becomes (0.0112×200 + 0.0388×100)/0.05 = 122.4. This is a dependence stress, not a change in either sleeve's individual loss law.

At λ = 1 the portfolio loses 200 with probability 0.04 and zero otherwise. ES is 160, but VaR falls to zero because F(0) is now 0.96. A falling VaR can accompany a more severe concentrated tail. It would be a mistake to prefer the common-event portfolio solely on that quantile.

For this particular mixture, Cov(IA,IB) = λp(1−p), and both indicator variances are p(1−p), so their correlation is λ. That convenient equality comes from the specified construction. A correlation number generally does not identify a joint law or nonlinear portfolio tails. Common collateral, borrower sectors, margin calls and forced sales can create dependence mechanisms absent from an estimated covariance matrix. Conversely, invented stress probabilities should not be described as measured frequencies.

Scenario analysis can be useful without probabilities: report the loss and cash needs under each coherent shock, name the shock construction and avoid calling their arithmetic average an expected loss. Probability-weighted ES additionally requires a defensible joint probability law. Recomputing a portfolio under several plausible laws is a sensitivity analysis; it is not automatically a confidence interval or a theorem that reality lies between them.

6. Horizon scaling and heavy tails require assumptions

Suppose daily losses X1, …, Xh add to the horizon loss. This is already a substantive assumption: percentage returns compound; changing positions and nonlinear valuations need not sum as a frozen daily-loss process. If each daily mean is μ and the process has stationary covariances γk, expanding the variance of the sum gives

E[Lh] = hμ,
Var(Lh) = hγ0 + 2Σk=1h−1(h−k)γk.

There are h−k pairs k days apart, which proves the coefficient. If γ0 = σ² and every nonzero-lag covariance is zero, standard deviation is σ√h. Independence is sufficient, not necessary, for those zero covariances. Quantiles do not generally inherit a square-root rule from variance alone. Under joint normality, the sum is normal; with zα the standard-normal α quantile and φ its density,

VaRα(Lh) = hμ + σhzα,
ESα(Lh) = hμ + σhφ(zα)/(1−α).

For the ES formula, integrate xφ(x) from z to infinity and use φ′(x) = −xφ(x), giving φ(z). Adding the mean and scaling gives the result. If σh = 0 the loss is deterministic and both measures equal hμ; no conditioning on a positive-probability exceedance is needed. Even under iid normal losses, a nonzero mean grows like h while dispersion grows like √h. Multiplying the entire one-day VaR by √h therefore gets the mean term wrong.

Worked example 4 — Positive serial dependence

Let daily mean loss be zero and standard deviation be 2 CU. Stipulate Cov(Xt,Xt+k) = 4(0.3)k, as in a stationary AR(1) process; joint normality is an additional assumption. For ten days, the variance factor is 10 + 2Σk=19(10−k)0.3k = 17.346946006. Horizon variance is 69.387784024 CU² and standard deviation is 8.329933 CU. Ignoring dependence gives variance 40 and standard deviation 6.324555 CU.

At α = 0.99, z ≈ 2.326347874. Under the stated normal law, correct horizon VaR is 19.378322 CU and ES is 22.201056 CU; the independence VaR is only 14.713116 CU. This comparison isolates the stipulated covariance change. It does not establish that real losses are normal, AR(1), additive or constant in scale. Negative lag correlations can reduce horizon variance; the general covariance expression, rather than an automatic upward adjustment, governs the calculation.

Finite quantiles need not imply finite ES. Consider a positive Pareto loss with scale xm > 0 and tail P(L > x) = (xm/x)κ for x ≥ xm, κ > 0. Solving F(q) = α gives q = xm(1−α)−1/κ, finite for every α < 1. The continuous conditional tail density above q is κqκx−κ−1. Its first moment is κqκ∫q∞x−κdx, so ES = κq/(κ−1) for κ > 1 and is infinite for 0 < κ ≤ 1. This is an extended tail measure outside the earlier finite-integrable hypothesis, not a contradiction of it. For 1 < κ ≤ 2, ES exists but variance does not.

A finite historical sample always has a finite maximum and empirical ES. That does not establish a finite population tail mean. Extreme-tail estimates can be sensitive to a handful of observations, changing positions, dependence, truncation and distributional assumptions. Extra decimal places do not resolve those uncertainties. A risk report should preserve the source of its loss scenarios, the estimation window and the evidence for extrapolating beyond observed extremes.

7. Backtesting evaluates a forecast process, not a guarantee

Record a VaR forecast qt before each realized loss Lt is observed, with the same horizon, portfolio and cash convention. Define a strict exception It = 1{Lt > qt}. Under a specified null in which these indicators are independent Bernoulli variables with a known constant exception probability p, K = ΣIt is binomial:

P(K=k) = C(n,k)pk(1−p)n−k,
P(K ≥ kobs) = Σj=kobsnC(n,j)pj(1−p)n−j.

Choose the k exception dates in C(n,k) ways; independence gives the same product probability for each sequence, proving the formula. Under continuous correctly calibrated α quantiles p = 1−α. With atoms and strict exceptions, the true p may be smaller. Using p = 1−α as an exact null then needs justification; the quantile inequality alone does not supply independent Bernoulli trials. Conditional calibration P(It=1 | all past information) = p is a strong sufficient condition for that indicator sequence, by iterating conditional probabilities.

One-sided count probability asks whether there are unusually many exceptions under this predeclared null. It is neither the posterior probability that the model is wrong nor a measure of exception size. An unconditional count can also hide dependence: clustered violations and dispersed violations with the same count have the same binomial count statistic. Overlapping multi-day losses share underlying days, so treating their indicators as independent is generally unjustified. In-sample fitted forecasts, changed definitions and repeated window selection can also invalidate a nominal calculation.

Worked example 5 — Seven exceptions tell more than one story

For 250 predeclared one-day forecasts with iid null exception probability 0.01, expected exceptions are 2.5. If seven are observed, the exact upper count tail is approximately 0.01370145. It is evidence against this particular null at a predeclared 5% test size; rejecting the null does not isolate whether the cause is poor scale estimates, dependence, changed exposures, data errors or another failure.

Compare exceptions on days (20,50,80,110,140,170,200) with exceptions on days (40,41,42,43,44,45,46). Both have the same count tail. The first has no adjacent exception pairs and longest run 1; the second has six pairs and longest run 7. These two descriptive summaries do not by themselves come with a calibrated significance level. If an alarm for any run of seven exceptions was specified beforehand, the iid null bounds its probability by (250−7+1)0.017 = 2.44×10−12: each of 244 possible seven-day blocks has that all-exception probability, and the union bound does not require the overlapping blocks to be independent. This is a bound for the stated alarm, not a license to search freely across alarms and report only the smallest probability.

Changing each exception's loss from 20 to 200 CU without moving its date or crossing status leaves all these count and run statistics unchanged. Tail-severity assessment needs the magnitudes, forecast conditioning, full loss distribution and appropriate comparison criteria. A VaR coverage test is not an ES validation test. With zero exceptions in 100 iid trials at p = 0.01, the probability of that result is 0.99100 ≈ 0.3660; observing none is entirely compatible with the null and proves no absence of risk.

An honest review therefore reconciles positions and realized P&L first, examines unconditional coverage, time dependence and loss severity separately, and records exposure changes and model revisions. It uses prospective tests or adjusts for the actual selection procedure. Adequate backtesting on observed periods still cannot demonstrate that omitted crisis mechanisms, unavailable financing or unfamiliar market structures are harmless.

8. Reproduce a finite risk certificate

Download the original inputs, standard-library model, reference output, file manifest and instructions. Keep the model and input together and run:

python3 v11-c04-analysis.py
python3 v11-c04-analysis.py --input changed-inputs.json --output changed-output.json

The model reads exact decimal strings and calculates finite-scenario losses, VaR, ES, means, variances, atom diagnostics and attaining tail weights as exact fractions. It reports risk for each held component and for their sum under the same law. Signed holdings are allowed; the model reorders their resulting losses rather than multiplying a positive-position quantile by a negative number. It returns one tail optimizer when losses tie; the optimizer can change with row order while the risk values remain invariant.

Two separate diagnostic sections reproduce the stipulated serial-covariance normal calculation and binomial exception-count tail. Their floating results are labeled approximations. The latter also reports descriptive run and adjacent-pair counts, without claiming a general independence test. The program does not estimate physical probabilities, fit a time series, price securities, calculate legal capital or determine commercial risk limits. Changing model inputs creates a new stipulated case, not new empirical evidence.

For an independent check, derive the tail probabilities by hand, verify every selected mass is between zero and the supplied state mass, verify the selected mass sums to 1−α, and compare the weighted loss with f(q). Test a certain added loss, positive rescaling, a short position and the common-event dependence change. Each tests an economic property; successful reproduction of the reference output alone is not a validation argument.

Exercises

  1. New atom boundary. Losses −5, 20 and 80 have probabilities 0.80, 0.15 and 0.05. Find mean, 90% VaR and ES, strict and weak conditional means at VaR. Find 95% VaR/ES and explain what happens when α increases from 0.95 to 0.9501.
  2. Threshold minimization. Use worked example 2 at α = 0.90. Derive f on the intervals between its three losses, identify all minimizing thresholds and verify the minimum equals ES. Explain why a minimizer need not equal the left quantile.
  3. A dual certificate and its scope. At α = 0.925 in worked example 2, verify the weights (0,1/3,2/3) and show that (0,1/2,1/2) gives a smaller feasible weighted loss. Prove finite ES subadditivity directly from the weight constraints. Identify what is missing if the two desks provide only their marginal laws.
  4. Dependence transfer. Keep each sleeve's loss probability at 0.04. In the common/independent mixture take λ = 0.50. Compute all four joint probabilities, the sum's 95% VaR and ES, and the indicator correlation. Compare with independence and explain whether the change is a forecast.
  5. Signs and units. For worked example 2 at α = 0.925 calculate VaR/ES of 2L+7 and of −L. Explain why positive homogeneity does not justify negating the reported VaR or ES. Interpret a certain 7-CU receipt instead of a loss.
  6. Revaluation versus cash. In worked example 1 let the sale-date yield fall to 2%. Compute the exact funded loss, its first-order approximation and their difference. If the bond cannot be pledged or sold until date1, is that favorable mark enough to meet tomorrow's6-CU payment? State a concrete additional resource that would change the answer.
  7. A different horizon. Three additive daily losses each have mean1 CU and standard deviation2 CU, with lag correlation (0.5)k. Derive the three-day mean and variance. Under joint normality compute 97.5% VaR and ES using z ≈ 1.959963985 and φ(z) ≈ 0.058445070. Name two assumptions whose failure invalidates that normal risk calculation even if the covariance arithmetic is right.
  8. Finite quantile, infinite tail. For a Pareto law with scale1 derive the95% quantile and ES when κ = 2. Repeat the existence analysis at κ = 0.8. Explain why a finite250-observation historical ES cannot disprove the latter model's infinite population ES.
  9. Count, clustering and selection. Derive the iid binomial probability of zero exceptions in 100 days at p = 0.01. Explain what is and is not learned. For the two seven-exception histories in worked example5, calculate adjacent-pair counts, derive the stated run bound, and explain why picking the most dramatic result from many unreported tests changes its interpretation.
  10. Risk committee decision. A proposal says: “Each sleeve has95% VaR zero; adding them is safe. Last year's maximum loss was40, so ES cannot exceed40. A bank loan will cover all margin needs because terminal expected profits are positive.” Write a defensible response using one computed counterexample and a list of evidence needed for an actual decision. Distinguish physical-law risk, observed data limits, committed liquidity and authority to take risk.

Solutions and evaluation criteria

1. New atom boundary

Mean is 0.8(−5)+0.15(20)+0.05(80) = 3 CU. At 90%, VaR is20. The 0.10 tail includes 0.05 at80 and 0.05 at20, so ES = (4+1)/0.10 = 50. The strict conditional mean is80; the weak mean is (3+4)/0.20 = 35. At 95%, F(20)=0.95, so left VaR remains20 but ES is80. At 0.9501 VaR jumps to80 while ES remains80. Neither a negative ordinary loss nor an atom causes a mathematical problem when sign and quantile conventions are explicit.

2. Threshold minimization

The mean loss is5.5 and τ=0.10. For θ≤0, f(θ)=55−9θ. For 0≤θ≤10, f(θ)=θ+10[0.05(10−θ)+0.05(100−θ)]=55. For 10≤θ≤100, f(θ)=50+θ/2. For θ≥100, f(θ)=θ. Thus every θ in[0,10] minimizes f and the minimum is55. The left90% quantile is0. A minimization algorithm may return another threshold in the flat interval; that does not alter the ES objective or authorize changing the chapter's quantile definition.

3. Dual certificate

Capacities p/τ are(12,2/3,2/3). Both proposed vectors are nonnegative, sum to1 and satisfy the capacities. The first has value10/3+200/3=70; the second has5+50=55. For any common feasible w, Σw(L+M)=ΣwL+ΣwM≤ES(L)+ES(M); taking the maximum gives subadditivity. The maxima may be attained by different weights, which explains possible strict inequality. Marginal laws alone do not specify joint states pairing L and M, so they do not identify the distribution of the sum. One must supply and defend a joint law, not assume independent or perfectly aligned ranks silently.

4. Dependence transfer

At λ=0.5, both probability is0.5(0.04)+0.5(0.0016)=0.0208; each single-loss probability is0.5(0.0384)=0.0192; neither is0.9408. VaR is100 since0.9408<0.95. ES fills0.0208 at200 and0.0292 at100, giving(4.16+2.92)/0.05=141.6. Covariance of the indicators is0.0208−0.0016=0.0192; divide by0.04×0.96=0.0384 to obtain correlation0.5. The tail average rises from103.2 under independence while marginal ES stays80 each. This is a stipulated dependence sensitivity, not a forecast without evidence forλ.

5. Signs and units

For2L+7, positive scaling and a certain loss give VaR27 and ES147. For−L the ordered losses are−100 with mass0.05, −10 with mass0.05 and0 with mass0.90. The92.5% quantile is0, and the whole upper0.075 tail can be filled from the mass at0, so ES is0. Negating10 or70 would be wrong because shorting changes which states are the worst. A certain7-CU receipt means L−7, giving VaR3 and ES63 in the original loss units; it must actually be available under the chosen funded-loss convention.

6. Revaluation versus cash

The exact loss is100/1.05−100/1.02=−1000/357 ≈ −2.80112045 CU. With d=−0.03 the linear approximation is−400/147 ≈ −2.72108844. Their difference is−200/2499 ≈ −0.08003201, agreeing with the negative convexity remainder. This terminal economic gain is not cash available tomorrow. A committed facility drawable before the payment, a legally and operationally available collateral transaction, or unrestricted cash would change the funding analysis; each requires its actual amount, deadline, cost and conditions. An expected future gain alone is not such a resource.

7. A different horizon

Mean is3. Variance is4[3+2(2×0.5+1×0.25)]=22 CU²; standard deviation is√22. Normal VaR is3+1.959963985√22≈12.19305 CU; ES is3+√22(0.058445070)/0.025≈13.96527 CU. The supplied rounded normal values imply correspondingly rounded answers. Examples of material failures are nonlinear/compounded loss aggregation, changing holdings, nonstationary covariance or a nonnormal heavy-tailed joint law. Merely knowing the first two moments does not prove the normal formulas.

8. Pareto tail

At κ=2, q.95=(0.05)−1/2=√20≈4.472136 and ES=2q=2√20≈8.944272. The tail mean exists although variance is infinite at this boundary. At κ=0.8, the quantile is201.25, finite, but the tail-mean integral contains ∫q∞x−0.8dx and diverges. Every finite sample has a finite maximum almost surely, so its finite empirical tail mean is compatible with an infinite population mean. Rejecting that model requires a justified inferential procedure and data, not the finiteness of one statistic.

9. Backtesting

The single zero-exception sequence has probability0.99100≈0.36603234. Its occurrence is not unusual under the stated null and gives no bound on exception severity or omitted-state losses. The dispersed seven-event history has0 adjacent pairs and longest run1; the clustered history has6 pairs and longest run7. For each specified seven-day block, iid probability of seven exceptions is0.017; union over244 starts gives at most2.44×10−12. The union bound permits overlaps. If many thresholds, run lengths, windows and models were tried after observing data, the relevant selection event is broader than this one predeclared alarm. Preserve the full search procedure or use prospective validation; do not present a selected nominal probability as if no search occurred.

10. Risk committee criteria

The independent two-sleeve example gives individual 95% VaRs0 but portfolio VaR100 and ES103.2. A sample maximum40 bounds only that empirical sample's losses; it is not a bound on unseen population losses or future empirical estimates. Positive expected profits do not establish a committed facility, sufficient collateral, timely settlement or survival in a loss state. A strong response specifies holdings and horizon, physical joint-law evidence and dependence alternatives, full cash/mark reconciliation and tail sensitivity, limits of the sample, a dated margin/funding ladder and actual facility conditions. It then separates measured risk from a decision made under institutional risk appetite and authority. Several decisions can be defensible; credit depends on explicit evidence and workable conditions, not a forced approval or rejection.

Teach-back and delayed check

Teach-back. Explain to a colleague why the92.5% ES of the(0,10,100) case is70 rather than100 or55. Use exactly0.075 probability mass and show the boundary fraction. Then explain why neither70 nor the95% VaR of a different portfolio funds a payment tomorrow. A correct explanation distinguishes an average under a declared law from a dated, available resource.

Delayed check. Without looking back, reconstruct the four independent two-sleeve state probabilities; find the95% VaR/ES of the sum and each sleeve. Then state the dual-weight constraints and use them to prove subadditivity in three lines. Finally identify why seven clustered exceptions call for an additional diagnostic beyond a binomial count.

Delayed-check answer

The probabilities are(0.9216,0.0384,0.0384,0.0016). Each sleeve has VaR0/ES80; the sum has VaR100/ES103.2. Common weights satisfy w≥0, Σw=1 and wi≤pi/0.05. Bound the weighted sum of two losses by the two separate maxima, then maximize. The exception count discards dates and magnitudes, so equal counts can conceal clustering and different severity; any statistical claim about the additional diagnostic must state its own null and selection procedure.

Sources, limits and continuation

The primary method reference is Rockafellar–Uryasev, Conditional Value-at-Risk for General Loss Distributions, specifically the quantile/integrability definitions, atom adjustment, finite formula, threshold-minimization proof and coherent-risk discussion. The original cases, finite dual proof, cash conventions, covariance calculation and binomial/run derivations here are independently developed using the library's probability and finance prerequisites. The reference's portfolio-optimization applications are not claimed as covered. All implemented risk laws are supplied scenarios; a working program does not make them empirically correct.

Liquidity, funding and asset-liability management turns the cash-timing distinction into a dated ladder of funding gaps, collateral and contingent payments. Subsequent stress and governance chapters combine loss measurement with concentration, feasibility, escalation and institutional choices. Market-risk statistics are inputs to those decisions; they are not complete accounts of them.

The chapter supplies its own finite proof, dual certificate and original examples; no source portfolio application, empirical claim or current regulation is adopted.
